We need to find minimum sum of distinct positive integers array of length n such that no two distinct elements sum to k.

We can choose smallest possible numbers while avoiding pair sums equal to k.

This is reminiscent of greedy: we try to choose numbers from 1 upward, but if picking a number would cause a pair with an already chosen number to sum to k, we skip it.

Because we need distinct positives. The minimum sum will be achieved by picking the n smallest numbers possible that avoid any pair summing to k.

Observation: For each integer x, the forbidden counterpart is y = k - x. To avoid having both x and y in the array (if x != y). If x == y (i.e., k is even and x = k/2), then we cannot have two copies of that number (but since numbers are distinct, we can only have at most one copy of x anyway; so if we include x, we don't have another equal element to sum to k with itself? Actually the condition is pair of distinct elements that sum to k. So if we have only one occurrence of x = k/2, there is no distinct pair (since need two distinct elements). So we can include at most one of x = k/2. So we can treat that as normal: we cannot have both x and k-x if x != k-x; and we can have at most one of x if x = k/2.

Thus the problem reduces to selecting n distinct positive integers minimizing sum, such that we do not select both x and k-x for any x.

This is like we have pairs (x, k-x) for x < k-x. Plus possibly a singleton when k even and x = k/2.

We want to pick as many small numbers as possible, but we cannot pick both from a pair.

Thus greedy: iterate i from 1 upward; maintain a set chosen; for each i, if i is not forbidden (i.e., we haven't already chosen k-i), then we can take i; else skip i.

Because if we have already chosen k-i, then picking i would create a pair summing to k. Since we are going in increasing order, we will have chosen smaller numbers first; if k-i < i, then k-i would have been considered earlier and possibly chosen; if we chose it, we must skip i. If k-i > i, then we haven't considered it yet; we can safely choose i now, and later when we reach k
